claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructures with numerous internal boundaries.
Introducing a controlled amount of lattice distortion through high-pressure torsion can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
High-pressure torsion introduces lattice distortion in the alloy.
High-pressure torsion produces grain refinement in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Grain refinement and increased dislocation density enhance strength by creating more obstacles to dislocation motion.
Increased grain-boundary area and lattice strain promote more homogeneous deformation.
Increased grain-boundary area and lattice strain reduce the propensity for microcracking and thereby improve ductility.
A refined duplex microstructure that retains a lamellar character can produce an improved mechanical response in an eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The proposed HPT treatment will improve strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
Pressure and number of HPT turns must be optimized to avoid excessive grain refinement or defects that compromise ductility.
The optimal amount and distribution of lattice distortion depend on alloy composition and starting microstructure.
Room-temperature tensile strength and tensile ductility of HPT-processed material can be compared with those of an unprocessed control to test the hypothesis.
Failure of HPT processing to significantly improve both strength and ductility relative to the unprocessed material would falsify the hypothesis.
